sentences: Someone just fell in this room.
No camera saw it.
Nobody wore a sensor.
The Wi-Fi did.
In twelve minutes you'll know exactly how, down to the line of code that rang this alarm.
Picture an older person who lives alone.
They fall, and the phone is across the room.
Cameras feel like spying, and a wristband gets left on the nightstand.
So here is the question: can the room itself notice the fall?
Think of a pond.
Drop a stone, and ripples spread out and bounce off everything they meet.
Someone on the far bank can tell a reed is there, just from how the ripples arrive.
Radio waves do the same thing in a room.
Three small boards keep sending Wi-Fi messages to each other, and a body in the way changes how each wave arrives.
We never look at the person.
We watch the ripples wobble.
The radio's report of how each wave arrived is called CSI.
And Wi-Fi is not one wave.
It is 52 narrow waves sent side by side, like 52 radio stations.
For every message, the board measures how loud each station arrived.
So every message gives us 52 volume numbers, and about 33 messages arrive every second.
Each of those narrow waves is called a subcarrier.
Now squeeze all those numbers into one wiggly line, and compare three rooms.
An empty room: calm.
Someone walking: busy all the time.
A fall: busy, then one sharp jerk, then flat, because the person is lying still.
That shape is everything.
The whole program hunts for one sharp jerk, followed by stillness.
Let's follow one real fall through the code.
Each Wi-Fi message reaches the computer like a letter in an envelope.
138 bytes in total.
The first 10 are the address on the envelope: which board sent it, how strong it was, and when.
The other 128 are the letter itself: the readings.
Why two numbers per reading?
Draw each pair as an arrow on graph paper.
A pair of 30 and minus 40 means: 30 steps right, 40 steps down.
The arrow's length is 50, from the classic three, four, five triangle.
That length is how loud the station arrived.
The direction we simply throw away.
Next, think of the equalizer on a music player.
Slide down the very slow drift, like a room warming up.
Slide down the very fast hiss from the electronics.
Keep only the middle: wobbles about as fast as a human body moves.
But a jerk alone is not a fall.
You might just sit down hard.
So the detector works like a careful smoke alarm with stages.
Calm.
Something is moving.
A sudden jerk.
Then: wait, and watch.
Only if the person stays still does it ring.
Think of a restaurant.
The kitchen does the heavy cooking in the back, so the dining room never freezes.
In the app, the kitchen is a worker called FrameSource.
It runs the whole pipeline we just saw, and passes every finished result through a hatch, with a bell, to the window you look at.
Some numbers are not our choice.
Wi-Fi itself splits every message into 52 narrow waves.
That comes from the Wi-Fi standard, so every board sees the same stations.
The envelope size is our own format: an address, plus the readings.
And the message rate is simply measured.
It changed from one recording to the next, so the code never assumes a fixed rate.
It reads the real rate from every recording.
Other numbers are choices, and each one is a trade.
The filter keeps only wobbles as fast as a human body moves.
The steepness limit sits between two real lines: walking reached about 16.7, and the fall only just crossed it.
That margin is small, and we say so.
The still window is the other trade.
Shorter, and the alarm comes sooner, but sitting down may ring it.
Longer, and help comes later.
And some numbers are results.
Three real recordings went in: an empty room, someone walking, and one real fall.
All three came out right: no alarm, no alarm, alarm, about three seconds after the impact.
One surprise: the empty room had the steepest spike of all, from radio noise.
A separate check saw that the room was too quiet, and stopped the detector.
And one fall is not a statistic, so the thesis reports each recording, not percentages.
These choices were not invented here.
Earlier research showed that human activity changes the radio signal slowly, so fast changes are noise.
It showed that the signal changes caused by a body are correlated across all stations, so they can be merged into one line.
And it showed that after a fall, the signal goes from busy to stable.
Here are those sentences, highlighted in the original papers.
Picture this.
After lunch, someone walks to the bedroom and lies down for a nap.
If they lie down slowly, the motion line bends gently.
The steepness stays near two, far below the limit, and nothing rings.
But if they flop onto the bed, the line jumps in a split second, then goes flat while they sleep.
To the detector, that is a sharp jerk followed by stillness.
That is exactly the shape of a fall, so the alarm rings.
So how could we fix it?
Five ideas.
First, mark the bed as a zone where a fall needs more proof.
Second, put boards at different heights, to see if the body reached the floor.
Third, wait longer and check for breathing, because a sleeper breathes calmly.
Fourth, after a jerk, play a sound and let the person cancel it.
Fifth, use the clock: stillness in bed at night is just sleep.
We are not the first to meet this problem.
An earlier fall detector found that lying down and sitting down can look just like a fall.
And the breathing fix is not a guess: other research measured breathing with ordinary Wi-Fi.
Watches and pendants detect falls well, but people take them off to sleep or to charge them.
Cameras see everything, and that is the problem in a bedroom or a bathroom.
Radar sensors need no camera, but they need special hardware, at a few hundred dollars per room.
Wi-Fi products exist too, but their software is closed and sold by subscription.
This project uses three boards worth about fifteen dollars, its rules fit on one screen, and it needs no training data.
Research papers tell the same story.
An early system saw people through walls, but it needed special radios.
Later work showed that cheap boards like the ESP32 can read the same channel information.
And one warning applies to all of them: if Wi-Fi can sense you, an outsider might sense you too.
And the honest part.
This is a prototype: one room, one real fall, and no tests with older people.
The next steps are more recordings, more rooms, and a fix for the bed.
Ripples, radio stations, letters, a spreadsheet, three clean ups, one steep moment, and a careful alarm.
Plus a bed it can still confuse, and a cheap, open answer to expensive products.
That is the whole idea.
